claim: Genotype-based diagnostics for antibiotic resistance represent a promising alternative to empiric therapy, reducing inappropriate antibiotic use.
source: Genotype-based diagnostics for antibiotic resistance represent a promising alternative to empiric therapy, reducing inappropriate antibiotic use.
evidence: Supported by citations to other scholarly work

claim: The utility of genotype-based diagnostics will wane with the emergence of novel resistance.
source: However, because such assays infer resistance based on known genetic markers, their utility will wane with the emergence of novel resistance.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the nature of genotype-based diagnostics

claim: Maintenance of genotype-based diagnostics will require surveillance to ensure early detection of novel resistance variants.
source: Maintenance of these diagnostics will therefore require surveillance to ensure early detection of novel resistance variants, but efficient strategies to do so remain undefined.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the limitation of genotype-based diagnostics

claim: Patient characteristic-informed sampling is not a reliable strategy for efficient variant detection.
source: We show that patient characteristic-informed sampling is not a reliable strategy for efficient variant detection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations

claim: Sampling informed by pathogen characteristics, such as genomic diversity and genomic background, is significantly more efficient than random sampling in identifying genetic variants associated with resistance and diagnostic escape.
source: In contrast, sampling informed by pathogen characteristics, such as genomic diversity and genomic background, is significantly more efficient than random sampling in identifying genetic variants associated with resistance and diagnostic escape.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations

claim: Nucleic acid-based diagnostics that enable rapid pathogen identification and prediction of drug susceptibility profiles can improve clinical decision-making, reduce inappropriate antibiotic use, and help address the challenge of antibiotic resistance.
source: Nucleic acid-based diagnostics that enable rapid pathogen identification and prediction of drug susceptibility profiles can improve clinical decision-making, reduce inappropriate antibiotic use, and help address the challenge of antibiotic resistance (McAdams et al., 2019; Fingerhuth et al., 2017; Tuite et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: The sensitivity of nucleic acid-based diagnostics may be undermined by undetected genetic variants.
source: However, the sensitivity of such diagnostics may be undermined by undetected genetic variants (André et al., 2017; Berhane et al., 2018; Herrmann et al., 2008; Guglielmino et al., 2019; Whiley et al., 2011; Golparian et al., 2012; Bruisten et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2018a; Marks et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Pathogen surveillance programs aimed at early detection of novel variants are crucial to ensuring the clinical utility and sustainability of genotype-based diagnostics.
source: Pathogen surveillance programs aimed at early detection of novel variants are crucial to ensuring the clinical utility and sustainability of these diagnostics.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the limitations of genotype-based diagnostics

claim: Use of traditional nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for pathogen identification and genotype-based diagnostics for antibiotic resistance can select for genetic variants that escape detection.
source: Use of traditional nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for pathogen identification and genotype-based diagnostics for antibiotic resistance can select for genetic variants that escape detection (Smid et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Mutations and/or deletions at the NAAT target locus that cause an amplification failure have arisen in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Staphylococcus aureus, and Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Mutations and/or deletions at the NAAT target locus that cause an amplification failure have arisen in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Staphylococcus aureus, and Plasmodium falciparum, resulting in false negative diagnostic errors only detected when using another diagnostic platform (Berhane et al., 2018; Herrmann et al., 2008; Guglielmino et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Diagnostic escape associated with genotype-based diagnostics for antibiotic resistance are the result of resistance-conferring variants not accounted for in the diagnostic's panel of resistance markers.
source: Diagnostic escape associated with genotype-based diagnostics for antibiotic resistance are the result of resistance-conferring variants (e.g., mutations or accessory genes) not accounted for in the diagnostic's panel of resistance markers (André et al., 2017) and require phenotypic testing to be uncovered.
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work and logical inference

claim: A framework was previously presented to quantify the sampling rate for early detection of novel antibiotic resistance variants.
source: We recently presented a framework to quantify the sampling rate for early detection of novel antibiotic resistance variants, defining the number of isolates that would need to undergo confirmatory phenotyping from those predicted by genotype to be susceptible (Hicks et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by reference to prior work by the authors

claim: The real-world application of the unbiased sampling model may be challenging for pathogens with high case incidence, such as N. gonorrhoeae, as the cost of phenotyping required by this model for timely detection of novel resistance variants is likely to be high.
source: The real-world application of this model may also be challenging for pathogens with high case incidence, such as N. gonorrhoeae, as the cost of phenotyping required by this model for timely detection of novel resistance variants is likely to be high (Hicks et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by reference to prior work and logical inference

claim: Novel variants may be more likely to emerge or spread in certain anatomical niches, demographics, or geographic regions.
source: Novel variants may be more likely to emerge or spread in certain anatomical niches, demographics, or geographic regions (Lewis, 2013; Collignon et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2019; Hernando Rovirola et al., 2020), some of which may be systematically under-sampled (Kirkcaldy et al., 2019) and thus may provide a basis for sampling priority.
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Isolates or clades that are genetically divergent from the majority of isolates in a population may reflect travelers, their contacts, or otherwise under-sampled lineages.
source: Isolates or clades that are genetically divergent from the majority of isolates in a population may reflect travelers, their contacts, or otherwise under-sampled lineages (Perrin et al., 2003; Pham Thanh et al., 2016; Kingsley et al., 2009; Mac Aogáin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Some pathogen genomic backgrounds may be more conducive to the evolution of novel resistance mechanisms.
source: Some pathogen genomic backgrounds may be more conducive to the evolution of novel resistance mechanisms (Borrell and Gagneux, 2011), and markers of these genomic backgrounds (e.g., variants associated with a range of resistance mechanisms and/or resistance to other drugs) may help improve sampling efficiency.
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Given historical patterns of antibiotic use, novel resistance may emerge on a background of existing resistance.
source: Similarly, given historical patterns of antibiotic use, novel resistance may emerge on a background of existing resistance (Gould and MacKenzie, 2002).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: N. gonorrhoeae offers a useful model for testing sampling strategies, given the increasing drug resistance and recent focus on developing sequence-based resistance diagnostics.
source: Here, we test the performance of sampling strategies informed by these hypotheses using N. gonorrhoeae surveillance data. N. gonorrhoeae offers a useful model, given the increasing drug resistance and recent focus on developing sequence-based resistance diagnostics (Fingerhuth et al., 2017; Hook and Kirkcaldy, 2018).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Isolates from men and men who have sex with men (MSM) were overrepresented in datasets 1 and 2 compared to overall gonorrhea incidence in men and MSM in the US and Australia, respectively, during the study periods.
source: Isolates from men and men who have sex with men (MSM) were overrepresented in datasets 1 and 2 compared to overall gonorrhea incidence in men and MSM in the US and Australia, respectively, during the study periods (Supplementary file 2A, p<0.001 for both datasets by chi-squared test of men vs. women and MSM vs. non-MSM in dataset vs. reported incidence).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the datasets

claim: Dataset 4 was comprised exclusively of isolates from men.
source: Dataset 4 was comprised exclusively of isolates from men (Yahara et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by reference to the dataset source

claim: Pharyngeal isolates represented 4% and 18% of isolates with reported anatomical site of collection in datasets 1 and 2, respectively.
source: While it is difficult to estimate the prevalence of pharyngeal gonococcal infections, as they tend to be asymptomatic (Wiesner et al., 1973), pharyngeal isolates represented 4% and 18% of isolates with reported anatomical site of collection in datasets 1 and 2, respectively.
evidence: Supported by data from the datasets

claim: The geographic distribution of isolates in dataset 3 was significantly different from the reported case incidence across countries.
source: Similarly, the geographic distribution of isolates in dataset 3 was significantly different from the reported case incidence across countries (Supplementary file 2A, p<0.001 by chi-squared test of prevalence for each of the countries in dataset 3 vs. the reported overall incidence for each of the countries).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the dataset

claim: The detection efficiency was not improved by demography-, niche-, geography-aware sampling compared to random sampling for any of the resistance variants.
source: The detection efficiency was not improved by demography-, niche-, geography-aware sampling compared to random sampling for any of the resistance variants (Supplementary file 2B, Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations shown in Figure 1

claim: In several cases, detection efficiency significantly decreased in demography- or geography-aware sampling compared to random sampling, reflecting enrichment of the resistance variant in the overrepresented demographic or geographic region.
source: In several cases, detection efficiency significantly decreased in demography- or geography-aware sampling compared to random sampling, reflecting enrichment of the resistance variant in the overrepresented demographic or geographic region.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations

claim: No significant association between a given resistance variant and demographic group was observed across both dataset 1 and dataset 2.
source: However, no significant association between a given resistance variant and demographic group was observed across both dataset 1 and dataset 2, and no demographics or geographic regions were significantly enriched for all variants (Supplementary file 1), suggesting that preferential sampling of any of these demographics or geographic regions would not be a reliable strategy for increasing novel variant detection efficiency.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the datasets

claim: penA XXXIV was significantly enriched in MSM compared to men who have sex with women and women who have sex with men (MSW/WSM) in dataset 2.
source: For example, while penA XXXIV was significantly enriched in MSM compared to men who have sex with women and women who have sex with men (MSW/WSM) in dataset 2 (p<0.003, Fisher's exact test), there was no significant difference in the proportions of MSM and MSW/WSM with penA XXXIV in dataset 1 (p=0.461, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the datasets

claim: There was no significant difference in the proportions of MSM and MSW/WSM with penA XXXIV in dataset 1.
source: For example, while penA XXXIV was significantly enriched in MSM compared to men who have sex with women and women who have sex with men (MSW/WSM) in dataset 2 (p<0.003, Fisher's exact test), there was no significant difference in the proportions of MSM and MSW/WSM with penA XXXIV in dataset 1 (p=0.461, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the datasets

claim: The AZM-R-associated RplD G70D mutation in dataset 3 was at highest prevalence in patients from Malta and Greece (10% and 6.25%, respectively) and absent from patients from Denmark.
source: Similarly, while the AZM-R-associated RplD G70D mutation in dataset 3 was at highest prevalence in patients from Malta and Greece (10% and 6.25%, respectively) and absent from patients from Denmark, the AZM-R-associated 23S C2611T variant was at highest prevalence in patients from Denmark (5.45%) and absent from patients from Malta or Greece.
evidence: Supported by data from the datasets

claim: The AZM-R-associated 23S C2611T variant was at highest prevalence in patients from Denmark (5.45%) and absent from patients from Malta or Greece.
source: Similarly, while the AZM-R-associated RplD G70D mutation in dataset 3 was at highest prevalence in patients from Malta and Greece (10% and 6.25%, respectively) and absent from patients from Denmark, the AZM-R-associated 23S C2611T variant was at highest prevalence in patients from Denmark (5.45%) and absent from patients from Malta or Greece.
evidence: Supported by data from the datasets

claim: Isolates from patients with recent overseas sex were associated with significantly longer terminal branches compared to patients that had only engaged in sex locally.
source: Isolates from patients with recent overseas sex were associated with significantly longer terminal branches compared to patients that had only engaged in sex locally (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), in support of the hypothesis that international travel may be associated with the importation of novel or divergent strains, or, more generally, that isolates from travelers may be more likely to be associated with under-sampled lineages.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Preferentially sampling from patients with recent overseas sex significantly improved detection efficiency of the RplD G70D mutation and the penA XXXIV allele.
source: Preferentially sampling from patients with recent overseas sex significantly improved detection efficiency of the RplD G70D mutation and the penA XXXIV allele, as these were at marginally higher prevalence in isolates from patients with recent overseas sex compared to those from patients who had only engaged in sex locally (3.03% overseas vs. 0.98% local and 2.02% overseas vs. 1.67% local, respectively, p=0.090 and 0.683, respectively, by Fisher's exact test for both variants).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations and statistical analysis

claim: The 23S C2611T mutation was exclusively present in isolates from patients who had engaged in sex locally.
source: In contrast, the 23S C2611T mutation was exclusively present in isolates from patients who had engaged in sex locally (Supplementary files 1 and 2C).
evidence: Supported by data from the datasets

claim: The 23S C2611T mutation was marginally enriched in isolates from patients who had engaged in recent sex work compared to patients who had not.
source: Similarly, while the 23S C2611T mutation was marginally enriched in isolates from patients who had engaged in recent sex work compared to patients who had not (2.33% in sex workers vs. 1.31% in non-sex workers, p=0.327 by Fisher's exact test), and thus preferentially sampling from sex workers significantly improved detection efficiency of this variant compared to sampling from the full patient population, detection efficiencies for the RplD G70D mutation and the penA XXXIV allele were not significantly improved by preferentially sampling from sex workers (Supplementary files 1 and 2 C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the datasets

claim: Preferentially sampling from sex workers significantly improved detection efficiency of the 23S C2611T mutation compared to sampling from the full patient population.
source: Similarly, while the 23S C2611T mutation was marginally enriched in isolates from patients who had engaged in recent sex work compared to patients who had not (2.33% in sex workers vs. 1.31% in non-sex workers, p=0.327 by Fisher's exact test), and thus preferentially sampling from sex workers significantly improved detection efficiency of this variant compared to sampling from the full patient population, detection efficiencies for the RplD G70D mutation and the penA XXXIV allele were not significantly improved by preferentially sampling from sex workers (Supplementary files 1 and 2 C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations

claim: Detection efficiencies for the RplD G70D mutation and the penA XXXIV allele were not significantly improved by preferentially sampling from sex workers.
source: Similarly, while the 23S C2611T mutation was marginally enriched in isolates from patients who had engaged in recent sex work compared to patients who had not (2.33% in sex workers vs. 1.31% in non-sex workers, p=0.327 by Fisher's exact test), and thus preferentially sampling from sex workers significantly improved detection efficiency of this variant compared to sampling from the full patient population, detection efficiencies for the RplD G70D mutation and the penA XXXIV allele were not significantly improved by preferentially sampling from sex workers (Supplementary files 1 and 2 C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations

claim: While the distance maximization approach increased detection efficiency compared to random sampling for some variants, there were numerous instances in which this approach substantially decreased detection efficiency.
source: While the distance maximization approach increased detection efficiency compared to random sampling for some variants, there were numerous instances in which this approach, which led to preferential sampling of isolates associated with long branches, substantially decreased detection efficiency (Figure 2, Supplementary file 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations shown in Figure 2

claim: The clonal group sampling approach significantly decreased detection efficiency in only one instance (i.e., the 23S rRNA C2611T variant in dataset 4), where all isolates with the variant appeared in large clonal lineages of predominately variant-negative isolates.
source: The clonal group sampling approach significantly decreased detection efficiency in only one instance (i.e., the 23S rRNA C2611T variant in dataset 4, Supplementary file 2D), where all isolates with the variant appeared in large clonal lineages of predominately variant-negative isolates (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: The clonal group approach performed significantly better than random sampling for all diagnostic-associated variants across all datasets.
source: However, the clonal group approach performed significantly better than random sampling for all diagnostic-associated variants across all datasets.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations

claim: The relative performance of the clonal group sampling approach compared to random sampling was generally consistent across multiple thresholds based on pseudogenomes.
source: The relative performance of the clonal group sampling approach compared to random sampling was generally consistent across multiple thresholds based on pseudogenomes (i.e.,≤134 SNPs, ≤422 SNPs, and fastBAPS groups); relative performance of clonal group sampling using MLSTs, however, was less consistent and was significantly worse than random sampling for several variants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2D-E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Relative performance of clonal group sampling using MLSTs was less consistent and was significantly worse than random sampling for several variants.
source: The relative performance of the clonal group sampling approach compared to random sampling was generally consistent across multiple thresholds based on pseudogenomes (i.e.,≤134 SNPs, ≤422 SNPs, and fastBAPS groups); relative performance of clonal group sampling using MLSTs, however, was less consistent and was significantly worse than random sampling for several variants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2D-E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Multiple drug resistance is more common in pathogenic bacteria than one would expect from the product of frequencies of resistance to individual drugs.
source: Multiple drug resistance is more common in pathogenic bacteria than one would expect from the product of frequencies of resistance to individual drugs (Chang et al., 2015; Lehtinen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Novel resistance mechanisms might be more likely to arise and spread in bacterial strains that are already resistant to other drugs, a phenomenon that has been documented in N. gonorrhoeae.
source: This suggests that novel resistance mechanisms might be more likely to arise and spread in bacterial strains that are already resistant to other drugs, a phenomenon that has been documented in N. gonorrhoeae (Goldstein et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Ciprofloxacin was the recommended first-line therapy for uncomplicated gonorrhea through 2005 in the United Kingdom.
source: For example, as ciprofloxacin was the recommended first-line therapy for uncomplicated gonorrhea through 2005 in the United Kingdom (Whittles et al., 2018), 2007 in the United States (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 2007), and more recent years in other countries (Hemarajata et al., 2016; Unemo and Dillon, 2014; Bazzo et al., 2018), we investigated whether resistance to ESCs is significantly more likely to occur in the background of genotypic ciprofloxacin resistance (i.e., in strains with the GyrA S91F mutation).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Ciprofloxacin was the recommended first-line therapy for uncomplicated gonorrhea through 2007 in the United States.
source: For example, as ciprofloxacin was the recommended first-line therapy for uncomplicated gonorrhea through 2005 in the United Kingdom (Whittles et al., 2018), 2007 in the United States (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 2007), and more recent years in other countries (Hemarajata et al., 2016; Unemo and Dillon, 2014; Bazzo et al., 2018), we investigated whether resistance to ESCs is significantly more likely to occur in the background of genotypic ciprofloxacin resistance (i.e., in strains with the GyrA S91F mutation).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Mutations at positions 120 and/or 121 in PorB have been associated with resistance to a range of drugs from multiple classes.
source: Similarly, as mutations at positions 120 and/or 121 in PorB, the major outer membrane protein in gonococci, have been associated with resistance to a range of drugs from multiple classes (Mortimer and Grad, 2019), we investigated whether resistance to ESCs is significantly more likely to occur in strains with PorB 120 and/or 121 mutations.
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Isolates with CRO-RS and CFX-R were significantly more likely to have the GyrA S91F mutation and the PorB G120 and/or A121 mutations than the wild-type GyrA S91 or wild-type PorB G120/A121.
source: Isolates with CRO-RS and CFX-R were significantly more likely to have the GyrA S91F mutation and the PorB G120 and/or A121 mutations than the wild-type GyrA S91 or wild-type PorB G120/A121 (p<0.001, Fisher's exact test, Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3A–B

claim: Both GyrA S91F and PorB G120 and/or A121 mutations occurred across a range of ESC resistance locus haplotypes.
source: Further, both GyrA S91F and PorB G120 and/or A121 mutations occurred across a range of ESC resistance locus haplotypes (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C–D

claim: For all datasets with CRO-RS or CFX-R isolates, detection efficiency of both variants was significantly increased by only sampling isolates with the GyrA S91F mutation or the PorB G120 and/or A121 mutations.
source: For all datasets with CRO-RS or CFX-R isolates, detection efficiency of both variants was significantly increased by only sampling isolates with the GyrA S91F mutation or the PorB G120 and/or A121 mutations (Figure 3E–F, Supplementary file 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations shown in Figure 3E–F

claim: Preferential sampling of isolates with certain genetic markers, including markers of resistance to previous first-line antibiotics, may increase the detection efficiency of novel resistance variants.
source: Together, these results suggest that preferential sampling of isolates with certain genetic markers, including markers of resistance to previous first-line antibiotics, may increase the detection efficiency of novel resistance variants.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data

claim: With sequencing becoming more integral to routine pathogen surveillance and diagnostics, it is important to ensure that models mapping genotypic information to expected pathogen phenotype and/or clinical outcome are comprehensive and current.
source: With sequencing becoming more integral to routine pathogen surveillance and diagnostics, it is important to ensure that models mapping genotypic information to expected pathogen phenotype and/or clinical outcome are comprehensive and current (Donà et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: In the case of genotype-based diagnostics, sustained phenotypic surveillance is crucial for identifying resistance variants that have recently emerged and/or increased in prevalence from previously undetected levels.
source: In the case of genotype-based diagnostics, sustained phenotypic surveillance is crucial for identifying resistance variants that have recently emerged and/or increased in prevalence from previously undetected levels.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the nature of genotype-based diagnostics

claim: Availability and incorporation of information on pathogen characteristics (e.g., pathogen genomic data) into surveillance programs may ultimately decrease the cost of surveillance to maintain the sensitivity of diagnostic tools.
source: While effective incorporation of patient metadata into surveillance strategies may be challenging, availability and incorporation of information on pathogen characteristics (e.g., pathogen genomic data) into surveillance programs may ultimately decrease the cost of surveillance to maintain the sensitivity of these diagnostic tools.
evidence: Based on inference from the study results

claim: Collection of patient metadata, including demographic and geographic information, is crucial to understanding the epidemiology of drug resistance.
source: Collection of patient metadata, including demographic and geographic information, is crucial to understanding the epidemiology of drug resistance.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: It may be difficult to obtain data on the relevant patient features, and the predictive power of such features may rapidly decay because of patient mobility and interactions.
source: However, it may be difficult to obtain data on the relevant patient features, and the predictive power of such features may rapidly decay because of patient mobility and interactions (Goldstein et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Incorporation of WGS into routine pathogen surveillance by public health agencies may facilitate use of genomic information in phenotypic sampling strategies.
source: Incorporation of WGS into routine pathogen surveillance by public health agencies (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2019; Brown et al., 2019) may facilitate use of genomic information in phenotypic sampling strategies, particularly with emerging metagenomic approaches that do not require bacterial culture (Břinda et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: Phylogeny-aware sampling, particularly the clonal group approach, significantly improved detection efficiency over random sampling for multiple resistance and diagnostic-associated variants.
source: Our results show that phylogeny-aware sampling, particularly the clonal group approach, which reduces the amount of repeated sampling of closely related isolates, significantly improved detection efficiency over random sampling for multiple resistance and diagnostic-associated variants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations

claim: Identification of and preferential sampling of isolates with genetic markers that are consistently predictive of resistance across a range of mechanisms, including those associated with resistance to other drugs, may supplement phylogeny-aware sampling to further optimize detection efficiency of novel variants.
source: Further, identification of and preferential sampling of isolates with genetic markers that are consistently predictive of resistance across a range of mechanisms, including those associated with resistance to other drugs, may supplement phylogeny-aware sampling to further optimize detection efficiency of novel variants.
evidence: Based on inference from the study results

claim: The utility of sampling based on genetic markers of other resistance mechanisms will likely vary substantially across different drugs and be influenced by future treatment guidelines.
source: However, the utility of sampling based on genetic markers of other resistance mechanisms will likely vary substantially across different drugs and be influenced by future treatment guidelines.
evidence: Based on speculation about future applications

claim: It may be difficult to determine the most effective and reliable metric or threshold for clonal grouping, especially as this is likely to vary across different clinical populations, antibiotics, and bacterial species.
source: While the clonal group sampling approach increased detection efficiency for the resistance and diagnostic escape variants assessed here, it may be difficult to determine the most effective and reliable metric or threshold for clonal grouping, especially as this is likely to vary across different clinical populations, antibiotics, and bacterial species.
evidence: Based on speculation about practical implementation

claim: Detection efficiency was generally consistent across the two SNP thresholds and fastBAPS groupings based on WGS.
source: Detection efficiency was generally consistent across the two SNP thresholds and fastBAPS groupings based on WGS.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sampling simulations

claim: Performance of the clonal group approach using MLSTs was inconsistent and, in some instances, worse than random sampling, likely due to the shortcomings of MLST compared to WGS-based approaches in distinguishing between AMR variant-positive clades and more distantly-related variant-negative clades in species such as N. gonorrhoeae.
source: However, performance of the clonal group approach using MLSTs was inconsistent and, in some instances, worse than random sampling, likely due to the shortcomings of MLST compared to WGS-based approaches in distinguishing between AMR variant-positive clades and more distantly-related variant-negative clades in species such as N. gonorrhoeae (Harris et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and references to other scholarly work

claim: Surveillance incorporating WGS rather than MLST loci alone may further promote NAAT sustainability by enabling screening for variants with previously undetected mutations in target loci.
source: More broadly, surveillance incorporating WGS rather than MLST loci alone may further promote NAAT sustainability by enabling screening for variants with previously undetected mutations in target loci, such as the N. gonorrhoeae DR-9A G168A variants, that may be associated with diagnostic escape.
evidence: Based on inference from the study results

claim: Given the high degree of clonality among M. tuberculosis isolates and the significant variation in prevalence of drug resistance and resistance-conferring genotypes across clonal groups, the clonal group sampling approach may similarly improve detection efficiency of novel resistance variants in M. tuberculosis.
source: For example, given the high degree of clonality among M. tuberculosis isolates and the significant variation in prevalence of drug resistance and resistance-conferring genotypes across clonal groups (Merker et al., 2015; Casali et al., 2014), the clonal group sampling approach may similarly improve detection efficiency of novel resistance variants in M. tuberculosis.
evidence: Based on speculation supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: For species in which drug resistance is primarily acquired through gene acquisition, it is unclear if phylogeny-aware sampling based on the core genome will improve detection efficiency of novel variants.
source: For species in which drug resistance is primarily acquired through gene acquisition, it is unclear if phylogeny-aware sampling based on the core genome will improve detection efficiency of novel variants, though in gonococcus, there is evidence of a relationship between the core genome and the plasmid-borne resistance genes blaTEM and tetM (Sánchez-Busó et al., 2019), and it is further possible that, combined with core genome-based phylogeny-informed sampling, screening for homologs of known resistance genes from other species may expedite identification of any novel resistance genes acquired by the species of interest.
evidence: Based on speculation and references to other scholarly work

claim: In gonococcus, there is evidence of a relationship between the core genome and the plasmid-borne resistance genes blaTEM and tetM.
source: For species in which drug resistance is primarily acquired through gene acquisition, it is unclear if phylogeny-aware sampling based on the core genome will improve detection efficiency of novel variants, though in gonococcus, there is evidence of a relationship between the core genome and the plasmid-borne resistance genes blaTEM and tetM (Sánchez-Busó et al., 2019), and it is further possible that, combined with core genome-based phylogeny-informed sampling, screening for homologs of known resistance genes from other species may expedite identification of any novel resistance genes acquired by the species of interest.
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: The requirement of confirmatory phenotyping to identify novel resistance may not extend to pathogens that are expected to be associated with reliably-identifiable treatment failures.
source: Further, the requirement of confirmatory phenotyping to identify novel resistance may not extend to pathogens that are expected to be associated with reliably-identifiable treatment failures, as for these pathogens, identification of treatment failure likely represents the most efficient method of novel resistance variant detection (Berenger et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on logical inference and references to other scholarly work

claim: For pathogens such as N. gonorrhoeae, treatment failures may go undetected for reasons including partial abatement of symptoms or long treatment regimens.
source: However, for other pathogens, such as N. gonorrhoeae (Eyre et al., 2018), treatment failures may go undetected for reasons including partial abatement of symptoms or long treatment regimens.
evidence: Supported by references to other scholarly work

claim: As genotype-based diagnostics for antibiotic resistance become available for more species, it will be important to assess the efficiencies of these approaches across pathogens with different clinical, epidemiological, and evolutionary paradigms.
source: Ultimately, as genotype-based diagnostics for antibiotic resistance become available for more species, it will be important to assess the efficiencies of these approaches across pathogens with different clinical, epidemiological, and evolutionary paradigms.
evidence: Based on speculation about future research needs

claim: Any associations observed between the variants and patient or pathogen features do not necessarily reflect those around the time of emergence.
source: Since we lack the datasets to assess targeted sampling of variants from the time they first emerged in a population, any associations we observed between the variants and patient or pathogen features do not necessarily reflect those around the time of emergence.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the limitations of the study

claim: More longitudinal epidemiological and genomic studies, particularly after the implementation of genotype-based diagnostics, are necessary to better characterize patterns of novel resistance emergence and inform targeted surveillance approaches.
source: Thus, more longitudinal epidemiological and genomic studies, particularly after the implementation of genotype-based diagnostics, are necessary to better characterize patterns of novel resistance emergence and inform targeted surveillance approaches.
evidence: Based on speculation about future research needs

claim: The phylogeny-aware sampling approaches presented are based on the assumption that genomic data will be available for the pool of potential isolates from incident cases that may undergo confirmatory phenotyping.
source: The phylogeny-aware sampling approaches presented here are based on the assumption that genomic data will be available for the pool of potential isolates from incident cases that may undergo confirmatory phenotyping.
evidence: Based on the methods described in the study

claim: Using information on isolate features to increase surveillance efficiency may be feasible even in the absence of mass prospective sequencing.
source: However, using information on isolate features to increase surveillance efficiency may be feasible even in the absence of mass prospective sequencing.
evidence: Based on speculation about practical implementation

claim: Under the general assumption that novel resistance variants are more likely to appear in underrepresented lineages, phylogeny-aware surveillance could be paired with a diagnostic approach such as genomic neighbor typing.
source: For example, under the general assumption that novel resistance variants are more likely to appear in underrepresented lineages, phylogeny-aware surveillance could be paired with a diagnostic approach such as genomic neighbor typing (Břinda et al., 2020), where any isolates with either susceptible or low confidence calls that appear to be divergent from the genomes in the reference database would be prioritized for confirmatory phenotyping.

claim: A diagnostic that predicts AMR phenotypes through a combination of transcriptomic and genomic typing may facilitate targeted surveillance by identifying isolates with ambiguous predictions that could be prioritized for confirmatory phenotyping.

claim: SNP cutoffs tested for the clonal group approach included 134 SNPs and 422 SNPs.
